quoted_text.text:
### Transcript Exporter

A nightly job that exports closed-ticket transcripts from the helpdesk into the training
store. The exporter is the only writer to the training store; its job identity is the only
principal with write access to the bucket, granted through the platform's access policy.
Transcripts are exported in full, including customer names, email addresses, and complete
message bodies.

assessments.rationale: evd-005 shows that customers write ticket messages, and evd-002–evd-003 show that their messages are exported as transcripts into the training store and used as training data without redaction. This supports the applicability reasoning that the threat path involves untrusted customer ticket content flowing into the training pipeline rather than actions through a privileged administrative interface. However, the requirement text for req-ADMIN-001 and the full definition of thr-001 are not provided, so the conclusion that the requirement is not applicable cannot be fully validated.
missing_evidence: Authoritative specification of req-ADMIN-001, including its scope and conditions.
Full description of threat thr-001 to confirm that it does not involve administrative or operator interfaces.

assessments.rationale: evd-001 and evd-002 show that the system generates one suggested reply per open ticket for agents to review, with no description of multi-step or recursive agent loops or autonomous tool use. This supports the characterization of the system as a single-step suggestion generator. However, without the detailed conditions of req-AGENT-001 and the full threat description for thr-001, the determination that this requirement is not applicable remains an inference that requires confirmation.
missing_evidence: Full text of req-AGENT-001, including its applicability conditions for multi-step or recursive agents.
Complete definition of thr-001 to verify that it does not involve bounded agent execution scenarios.

assessments.rationale: evd-001, evd-002, and evd-005 jointly support that suggested replies are shown to internal support agents, who may edit or discard them and decide whether to use them, so every customer-facing response is mediated by a human. This aligns with the mapping’s premise that outputs are drafts published manually. However, without the normative text of req-AGENT-002 and a precise definition of what constitutes a high-impact action under that requirement, the conclusion that the requirement is not applicable still needs human confirmation.
missing_evidence: Authoritative specification of req-AGENT-002, including its criteria for high-impact actions without human publishing.
Full statement of thr-001 to ensure that its impact characteristics match the non-applicable condition described.

assessments.rationale: The available evidence (evd-001, evd-002) describes a model that generates text suggestions only; it does not mention tools or external services invoked autonomously by the model. This supports the mapping’s description of the system behavior. Nonetheless, determining that req-AGENT-003 is not applicable depends on that requirement’s precise conditions for tool invocation, which are not provided, so confirmation is needed.
missing_evidence: Full text of req-AGENT-003 describing when model-driven tool invocation controls apply.
Explicit documentation confirming that the Reply Service or model does not invoke external tools or services autonomously.

assessments.rationale: evd-002 and evd-004 describe internal components (Tuning Job, Training Store, Reply Service, artifact bucket) and do not mention external tool servers or tool protocols, supporting the claim that none are evident in the described architecture. missing_evidence: Authoritative description of req-AGENT-004 and its conditions for connecting models to external tool servers.
Architectural documentation clarifying whether any external tool servers are integrated beyond what is shown in the system overview.

assessments.rationale: evd-005 shows that customers write ticket messages; evd-002 shows these are exported as transcripts into the training store; and evd-003 states that what the customer wrote is what the model trains on. This directly supports the mapping’s factual premise that untrusted customer-authored content is used as model training data. Whether this satisfies the applicability conditions of req-AI-001 cannot be fully judged without that requirement’s specification, so the conclusion that req-AI-001 is applicable but unverified requires confirmation.
missing_evidence: Full specification of req-AI-001, including its conditions for applicability when using untrusted content as training data.

assessments.rationale: The evidence clearly shows that outputs are suggested replies shown to internal support agents, who can edit or discard them and decide whether to use them, so each customer-facing message is mediated by a human. However, concluding that req-AI-002 is not applicable depends on the requirement’s specific criteria for when human approval suffices, which we do not have, so a reviewer should confirm this mapping.

assessments.rationale: evd-001 and evd-002 show that suggested replies are rendered in an agent console UI, but the threat narrative in the mapping focuses on semantic poisoning of replies rather than markup-based or active-content attacks. This supports the idea that encoding controls for UI contexts would not directly mitigate the described model-behavior shift. Still, assessing that req-AI-004 is not applicable requires understanding that requirement’s exact focus on active content vs. semantic integrity, so confirmation is needed.
missing_evidence: Authoritative text of req-AI-004 describing its focus on active content, markup, or encoding requirements.
Threat thr-001 description explicitly distinguishing semantic poisoning from active-content exploits.

assessments.rationale: evd-005 shows that customers author ticket messages, which can be malicious yet still submitted as normal content; this supports the mapping’s claim that poisoning can occur regardless of how user authentication is delegated. However, evaluating non-applicability of req-AUTHZ-001 still depends on its formal criteria for tenant-aware authorization, which are not available.

assessments.rationale: evd-002 and evd-003 show that poisoning would occur through the normal production data path (helpdesk → Transcript Exporter → Training Store → Tuning Job). Still, whether req-CICD-001 is therefore not applicable cannot be firmly concluded without its detailed requirements.

assessments.rationale: evd-002 and evd-003 depict poisoning via legitimate jobs (Transcript Exporter, Tuning Job) processing malicious but normally submitted content, rather than unauthorized changes to deployment pipelines. This supports the gist of the mapping. However, without the text of req-OPS-004, we cannot fully validate the claim that it is not engaged by this threat.

assessments.rationale: evd-003 and evd-004 show a gradual model-updating process based on accumulated training data and weekly artifacts, which aligns with the mapping’s description of a gradual behavior shift rather than an acute alert-triggering event. Still, absent the text of req-OPS-005, we cannot definitively say that alert design and routing are irrelevant, so this mapping should be confirmed.

assessments.rationale: evd-002 and evd-003 describe how customer data is stored and used for training but do not discuss encryption in transit or at rest. The mapping’s claim that encryption would not mitigate this integrity-focused poisoning threat is plausible, yet assessing non-applicability of req-DATA-001 requires its formal objectives, which are not in the evidence.
missing_evidence: Full text of req-DATA-001, clarifying whether it is limited to confidentiality or also addresses integrity.
Documentation of encryption controls for the Training Store and artifact bucket, to understand how they relate to the threat.

assessments.rationale: evd-002 and evd-003 support that closed-ticket transcripts are exported in full and used for training, which is what enables poisoning. The mapping argues that defined retention periods do not directly affect this threat. While this is reasonable, without the text of req-DATA-002 it is not possible to fully validate that retention controls are irrelevant, so confirmation is needed.
